label: Weekend edition · Week of Oct 5–9
marketView: U.S. stocks closed the week at records, but the real story is rates and energy. The Iran war and now Hurricane Isaias have pushed oil up nearly 60% this year, headline inflation is heading back up, and the Fed, which hiked in September, is signaling one more hike by December. That drove the 10-year yield to its highest level since 2002. Leadership rotated into staples, utilities and energy while small caps fell, which tells me investors are bracing for higher-for-longer rates rather than chasing growth. Core inflation is still running near 2.5%, so the key question is whether the energy shock spreads. Wednesday's CPI and this week's big-bank earnings are the next tests.

stories.headline: 10-year Treasury yield hits its highest level since 2002
stories.summary: The 10-year yield touched about 5.35% on Wednesday, up roughly 60 basis points since late July, as sticky inflation, high energy costs and worries about federal debt pushed investors to demand more to lend long-term. The $39 billion 10-year auction priced at 5.300%, the highest auction yield since 2000. Bonds then rallied into Friday, and the broad bond index snapped a five-week losing streak.
stories.why: Almost every asset is priced off the risk-free rate. Higher long yields push up mortgage rates and corporate borrowing costs, squeeze equity valuations, and make leveraged buyouts harder to finance.
stories.interview: The story I'm watching is the long end of the curve. The 10-year got to 5.35% this week, the highest since 2002, driven by sticky inflation, the energy shock and deficit concerns. That's a headwind for LBO financing and for long-duration growth stocks, so I'm paying attention to how Treasury auctions clear.

stories.headline: Fed minutes point to another rate hike by year-end
stories.summary: Minutes from the September meeting show officials raised rates by a quarter point and most expect another increase will likely be needed before the end of the year. Markets put the odds of a December hike around 84%, versus about 17% for this month. Officials agreed inflation is too high but split on the reason to act: some see hikes as insurance, others want to stop energy- and AI-driven demand from spreading into broader inflation.
stories.why: The Fed is tightening in a year many expected cuts. That helps bank net interest income but pressures housing, credit and rate-sensitive stocks.
stories.interview: Unusually, the Fed is tightening into an energy supply shock. The September minutes signal one more hike by December, and futures agree. The internal debate is whether an oil-driven price spike turns into broader inflation, which is why Wednesday's CPI matters.

stories.headline: Hurricane Isaias knocks out ~63% of Gulf oil output on top of the Iran war shock
stories.summary: By Thursday, producers had shut in about 1.28 million barrels a day, roughly 63% of Gulf offshore oil, plus 57% of gas output. Isaias strengthened to Category 3 and was forecast to hit the Alabama–northwest Florida coast late Friday or early Saturday, with about 500,000 barrels a day of refining capacity near its path. It arrives with U.S. diesel stocks at their lowest seasonal level since EIA records began in 1982 and oil up nearly 60% this year as the Iran war constrains tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
stories.why: Energy is the channel from geopolitics to inflation to the Fed. Watch how quickly platforms and refineries restart this week; a slow recovery means higher fuel prices into winter.
stories.interview: Energy is the swing factor for everything else right now. Oil is up almost 60% this year because of the Iran war, and Isaias just took nearly two-thirds of Gulf production offline while diesel inventories are at record seasonal lows. That feeds straight into headline inflation and the Fed's next move.

stories.headline: Big-bank earnings kick off Tuesday with JPMorgan, Goldman and Wells Fargo
stories.summary: Third-quarter bank results start Tuesday with JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs and Wells Fargo, followed by Bank of America, Morgan Stanley and BlackRock on Wednesday. Analysts expect JPMorgan to earn about $5.90 a share on $51.3 billion of revenue, with net interest income up around 12% but trading revenue down about 18%.
stories.why: Bank results are the best read on deal flow, trading activity and credit quality. Higher rates are boosting lending income while volatility and a tougher financing backdrop weigh on other businesses.
stories.interview: Bank earnings this week will show the trade-off higher rates create. Net interest income should be strong, but trading is expected to be down year over year. I'll be listening for what management says about the M&A and IPO pipeline and whether credit losses are starting to rise.

stories.headline: Delta slashes its 2026 profit outlook on a $6 billion fuel bill
stories.summary: Delta cut its full-year earnings forecast to $5.10–$5.60 a share from $6.50–$7.50 and now expects fuel costs to rise about $6 billion this year. Third-quarter adjusted EPS of $1.72 narrowly missed estimates as fuel expense jumped 62% to $4.1 billion. Demand is still strong and fares are up about 25% from a year ago, but the airline expects fuel to cost $4.25 a gallon in the fourth quarter.
stories.why: This is one of the first big reads on how the energy shock hits corporate margins, and a test of how much higher prices consumers will absorb.
stories.interview: Delta is a clean case study in pricing power against input costs. Fares are up about 25%, demand is holding, but a $6 billion fuel increase still forced a big guidance cut. The question for the rest of earnings season is which companies can keep passing costs through.

stories.headline: S&P 500 sets a record, but defensive sectors led the way
stories.summary: The S&P 500 rose 1.2% for the week to 7,811.54 after hitting a record earlier in the week, and is up about 14% this year. Consumer staples, utilities and energy each gained close to 4%, while technology and industrials slipped and the Russell 2000 small-cap index fell 0.9%.
stories.why: When defensives and energy lead a rally, investors are positioning for higher rates and slower growth rather than a broad risk-on move. Small caps lagging fits that picture, since they are most exposed to borrowing costs.
stories.interview: Indexes are at records, but the leadership tells you more than the level. Staples, utilities and energy led while small caps fell, which looks like investors hedging against higher-for-longer rates rather than betting on growth.

stories.headline: Samsung and TSMC post huge AI-driven numbers, and their stocks barely react
stories.summary: Samsung guided to a record third-quarter operating profit of about 107 trillion won (roughly $80 billion), slightly above estimates, but revenue fell short of consensus and its shares closed 2.4% lower. TSMC said third-quarter sales rose about 50%, ahead of expectations. TSMC reports full results and guidance on Thursday.
stories.why: The AI buildout is still accelerating, but expectations are so high that beats alone no longer move the stocks. Guidance is what matters now.
stories.interview: AI demand is clearly still accelerating: Samsung just posted a record $80 billion quarterly profit and TSMC sales are up 50%. But both stocks barely moved, which tells you the good news is priced in. TSMC's guidance on Thursday is the next real signal.

stories.headline: Consumer sentiment slides to a five-month low as inflation expectations rise
stories.summary: The University of Michigan's preliminary October index fell to 46.3. Year-ahead inflation expectations rose to 4.7% and long-run expectations to 3.5%. The drop was steepest among lower-income households, and respondents cited high prices, energy costs and borrowing costs.
stories.why: Rising inflation expectations are exactly what the Fed worries about, and a squeezed consumer is a risk for spending, which drives most of the U.S. economy.
stories.interview: Consumer sentiment is near historic lows and inflation expectations are creeping up, with year-ahead expectations at 4.7%. That gives the Fed less room to pause and is a warning sign for consumer-facing companies heading into the holidays.
